questions.question: How do non-smokers split into separable charge bands, and what role do BMI and children sizing play in those clusters?

answer.value: With smokers cleared out, the k-means overlay carves non-smokers into low-, mid-, and high-charge tiers that line up with BMI: heavier BMIs drift upward on charges while family size (point size) nudges the cloud so that bigger households lean toward the pricier band. It is not a single clean line—there is overlap—but the clusters read as BMI-driven cost tiers with children acting as a secondary spread.

key_insights: Three color clusters emerge among non-smokers after zooming and filtering.
Higher BMI tracks higher charges within those clusters; children size modulates but does not override the BMI gradient.

reasoning.reasoning: Magnifies the dense BMI–charges band where non-smokers overlap.
Removes smoker rows so clustering reflects non-smoker structure.
Labels risk tiers that line up with BMI/children cues.
